newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Tougher EU Cuba stance adds to Madrid-Havana row.
newsitem.headline: Tougher EU Cuba stance adds to Madrid-Havana row.

text.p: The European Union has agreed to toughen its policy towards Cuba in a move likely to exacerbate worsening relations between Havana and Spain, diplomats said on Thursday.
The new policy, due for formal adoption on Monday, comes as Cuba has accused EU member Spain of meddling in its affairs and has withdrawn official approval for a new Spanish ambassador.

"The European Union will seek out opportunities -- even more actively than heretofore -- to remind the Cuban authorities, both publicly and privately, of fundamental responsibilities regarding human rights, in particular freedom of speech and association," an official EU policy paper says.
The bloc also pledged to intensify talks with the Cuban authorities and other sectors of society, "to promote respect for human rights and real progress towards pluralist democracy".
The policy change will add to tensions which have simmered for weeks between Havana and Madrid over criticism aimed at Cuba's one-party communist system by Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.

Cuba insisted on Wednesday that it would not change under pressure from anyone but played down tensions on the day of an annual, government-organised rally to commemorate students killed last century under Spanish rule.
Havana appeared keen to prevent any disturbances around the Spanish embassy, mounting a huge security operation and denying rumours among Cubans that Spain had changed its visa policy for Cubans.

European Union leaders have been under pressure from the United States to strengthen their stance towards Havana, which Washington hit with tougher economic sanctions this year after two U.S. civilian aircraft were shot down by Cuba in March.
"This will be a signal to Cuba and also to Washington that the EU is doing something on Cuba," one EU diplomat said of the new policy stance.

The United States and the 15-country EU have repeatedly clashed on Cuba policy since the aircraft were downed, with Washington passing laws intended to punish foreign investors who "traffic" with nationalised properties on the island.
Under the Helms-Burton law, named after its sponsors, top executives and major shareholders of firms found to be "trafficking" are to be barred from the United States.
Washington says its citizens never received compensation for assets seized by Cuban President Fidel Castro since 1959, so it treats them as stolen properties.
The EU says its position on the Helms-Burton law remains unchanged.
"It is not EU policy to try to bring about change by coercive measures with the effect of increasing the economic hardship of the Cuban people," it said.
The U.S. State Department has praised Spain for criticising human rights practices in Cuba.
"We're obviously very pleased that a European leader is now standing up to defend human rights and democracy in Cuba," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday.
